title: Newton's laws of motion
question: What are Newton's laws of motion?

principle.name: Newton's laws of motion
principle.formulaNote: force = mass × acceleration: things keep moving until a force acts, a force changes motion in proportion to mass, and every force has an equal and opposite partner
principle.idea: Things keep doing what they are doing, staying still or moving in a straight line, unless a force pushes or pulls them. A force changes motion more for light things than heavy ones (F = m × a), and whenever you push on something, it pushes back on you just as hard.
principle.discovered: 1687 · Isaac Newton, Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (London); F = ma written as an equation by Leonhard Euler, 1750

examples.title: Seat belts and crumple zones
examples.text: In a 50 km/h crash the car stops in under a tenth of a second, but you keep going. A belt that stops you over 90 cm instead of 5 cm cuts the force on you more than ten times: F = Δp ÷ Δt.

examples.title: Car against motorcycle off the line
examples.text: About 6,900 N on 1,300 kg and 1,100 N on 215 kg give both roughly 5 m/s². Once moving, power-to-weight rules: 85 W/kg for the car, 48 for a 150 cc motorcycle.

examples.title: Leaning into a bend
examples.text: Turning needs a push towards the centre of m × v² ÷ r from the tyres. A rider leans until tan θ = v² ÷ gr: about 26° at 50 km/h round a 40 m bend.

examples.title: Dishwasher spray arms
examples.text: The slanted jets push water out backwards, and the water pushes the arm forwards. Ten nozzles at half a bar spin it at about 35 rpm with no motor at all.

examples.title: The washing machine's spin
examples.text: At 1,200 rpm the drum wall must push the clothes inward at about 400 g. Water slipping through the holes gets no push, so it flies straight off along the tangent.

examples.title: A fan pushes back
examples.text: Blades throw air forward, and the air pushes the fan back: about 3 N for a desk fan on high. A 1,200 mm ceiling fan hangs about 1.3 kg lighter when it runs.

examples.title: The piano hammer flies free
examples.text: The jack lets the hammer go about 2 mm before the string, so it arrives by inertia alone. It touches the string for about 2 ms and bounces straight off.

examples.title: An unbalanced mixer blade
examples.text: A spinning lump needs m × r × ω² to keep it circling. Just 1 gram at the blade tip at 17,000 rpm pulls with about 110 N, so blades must be balanced.

examples.title: The CT scanner's spinning gantry
examples.text: An X-ray tube whirling round the patient every 0.35 s needs a centripetal push of about 20 g; the fastest scanners, at 0.25 s a turn, need nearly 40 g.

examples.title: Rockets and walking
examples.text: A rocket throws its exhaust backwards and is thrown forwards, even in empty space. When you walk, your foot pushes the ground back and friction pushes you forward.

hook: Three rules written in 1687 still run every car, fan, dishwasher and spacecraft. Push a puck on frictionless ice, crash-test a car with and without a seat belt, race a car against a motorcycle, and find out where Newton finally breaks.

explainer.title: Three rules for motion
explainer.text: Things keep still or keep moving in a straight line unless a force acts (inertia). A force makes them accelerate: a = F ÷ m. And forces come in pairs: push on something and it pushes back just as hard.

explainer.title: You keep going when the car stops
explainer.text: In a crash the car stops in under a tenth of a second, but you carry on. A seat belt stretches your stop over about 90 cm; without one you stop in centimetres against the wheel, with more than ten times the force.

explainer.title: Force, mass and power on the road
explainer.text: Off the line a car and a motorcycle accelerate about the same, around 5 m/s². Once moving, power-to-weight decides who pulls away. Turning needs a sideways push too, m v² ÷ r, which is why riders lean.

explainer.title: Every push pushes back
explainer.text: A dishwasher's spray arm spins because its slanted jets push it round. A fan throws air forward and is pushed back, and a rocket throws its exhaust out behind and is thrown forward, even in space.

explainer.title: Where Newton breaks
explainer.text: Near light speed momentum is γmv, not mv; inside atoms quantum mechanics takes over; in a spinning drum a fake centrifugal force appears. And heavy things don't fall faster: on the Moon, a hammer and a feather land together.

concepts.def: The way matter resists any change in its motion. More mass means more inertia.
A push or a pull, measured in newtons. One newton gives 1 kg an extra 1 m/s every second.
How quickly velocity changes, in m/s every second. Turning is acceleration too.
Mass × velocity. Forces change it, and in any push between two things it is shared, never lost.
Force × time, equal to the change in momentum. A longer stop needs a smaller force.
Two equal and opposite forces that two objects exert on each other.
The push towards the centre that keeps anything moving in a circle: m v² ÷ r.
A point of view that isn't accelerating or spinning, where Newton's laws hold as written.
